results.blind_working: Constant colour, constant pressure and faster attainment with a catalyst fit a static state too. Deuterium appearing in NH3 shows forward and backward reactions are still occurring, so equilibrium is dynamic.
Equilibrium needs a closed system so no species escape, and constant temperature so K stays fixed.

Experiment 1: x = 0.8, so HI = 1.6 mol and K = 1.6^2/(0.2*0.2) = 64. 2.0 mol HI corresponds to 1 mol H2 + 1 mol I2, so the same equilibrium is reached and HI = 1.6 mol. Check: HI = 2-2y with y = 0.2 gives (1.6)^2/(0.2)^2 = 64.
Deuterium scrambling into ammonia happens because forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. Both statements are true and R explains A.
A catalyst speeds forward and backward reactions equally, so the amount of product at equilibrium is unchanged and I is false. II correctly describes dynamic equilibrium.
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure.
Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on temperature, not on volume or the amount of liquid. Liquid remains, so the pressure is restored to 3.17 kPa.
Liquid water occupies less volume than ice. By Le Chatelier's principle, higher pressure favours the smaller volume, so some ice melts.
A is melting/freezing (II). B is evaporation/condensation (I). C is sublimation equilibrium (IV). D is dissolution/crystallisation (III).

A is true: vapour pressure is independent of the amount of liquid. B is true: water boils at 373 K at 1.013 bar. C is true as NCERT lists camphor and NH4Cl as subliming solids, though NH4Cl actually decomposes. D is false: at equilibrium the two rates are equal. E is false: vapour pressure depends only on temperature.
By Henry's law, p = K_H·x at constant T, so x is directly proportional to the partial pressure p.
Mass dissolved is proportional to pressure. Tripling the pressure (1.5 to 4.5 bar) triples the mass: 0.30 × 3 = 0.90 g.
A is true: high CO2 pressure increases its solubility. R is false: since x = p/K_H, a higher K_H means lower solubility at the same pressure.
Statement I is correct: gas solubility falls with temperature, so K_H rises. Statement II is correct: NH3 and HCl react with water and deviate from Henry's law.
By the law of mass action, Kc is products over reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient: [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3).
Reversing the reaction gives 1/16. Halving the equation takes the square root: (1/16)^(1/2) = 0.25.
Qc = (0.2)(0.2)/0.5 = 0.08. Since Qc > Kc = 0.04, the net reaction proceeds backward.
Reversing gives 1/K, multiplying by 2 gives K^2, dividing by 2 gives K^(1/2), and adding reactions gives K x K2. So A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

A is false because a catalyst does not change K. B is true because pure solids are omitted. C is true because a small K means reactants predominate. D is false because K depends only on temperature. E is true because Q < K drives the forward reaction.
Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, so Kp = Kc at all temperatures only when Δn_g = 0. For N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, Δn = 2 − 2 = 0. The other options have Δn = −1, +1 and +1.
With α = 0.5, total moles = 1 + α = 1.5. Each partial pressure is (0.5/1.5) × 3 = 1 atm. Kp = (1 × 1)/1 = 1.0 atm.
Δn_g = 2 − 0 = 2, so A is false. R is true because pure solids are excluded from Δn_g.
Statement I: Kc = [N2O4]/[NO2]^2 has units L mol^-1, so I is incorrect. Statement II: Δn = −2, so Kp = Kc/(RT)^2 with RT = 41.05, giving Kp < Kc; II is incorrect.
Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, a positive ΔG° gives ln K < 0, so K < 1 and reactants predominate at equilibrium.
ΔG = RT ln(Q/K). Here Q (10) > K (4.0), so ΔG > 0 and the net reaction runs in reverse until Q = K.
A: ΔG° < 0 gives K > 1 (III). B: ΔG° = 0 gives K = 1 (I). C: ΔG = 0 means equilibrium, Q = K (II). D: ΔG > 0 means the reverse reaction is spontaneous (IV).

A is true. B is false: at equilibrium ΔG = 0, not ΔG°. C is true: ΔG° depends on T, so K changes with T. D is true: K = 1 gives ΔG° = 0. E is false: if Q < K, the forward reaction proceeds even when ΔG° > 0. Correct set is A, C, D.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. It leaves K and the equilibrium position unchanged and only shortens the time taken to reach equilibrium.

At constant pressure, adding argon increases the volume and lowers the partial pressures. The equilibrium shifts toward more gas moles (Δn = +1), i.e. forward, so dissociation of N2O4 increases. K is unchanged.
Δn(gas) = 0, so pressure has no effect and A is true. NO formation is endothermic, so R is true. However, R concerns temperature and does not explain the pressure behaviour in A.
Compression increases the NH3 yield, but K depends only on temperature, so I is incorrect. Inert gas at constant volume leaves partial pressures unchanged, so there is no shift and II is correct.
BF3 is electron-deficient, so it accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid). It has no proton to donate, so it is not a Bronsted acid. HCl and H2O are Bronsted acids, and NH3 is a base.
NH3 gains a proton to become NH4+, giving the pair NH4+/NH3. H2O loses a proton to become OH-, giving the pair H2O/OH-.
HCO3- can donate a proton (forming CO3^2-) or accept one (forming H2CO3), so it is amphiprotic.

A is true: NH3 accepts H+ from water. R is true: a proton acceptor must donate an electron pair to H+, so it is a Lewis base. R is only a general classification fact and does not explain why NH3 accepts a proton.
Statement I is correct: Cl- is a very weak conjugate base. Statement II is incorrect: Ag+ is a Lewis acid but has no proton to donate, so it is not a Bronsted acid.
With alpha << 1, [H+] = sqrt(Ka*c) = sqrt(1.0e-5 * 0.1) = sqrt(1.0e-6) = 1.0e-3 M.
Across period 2 the electronegativity of the central atom rises (C < N < O < F), so the X–H bond becomes more polar and acid strength increases: CH4 < NH3 < H2O < HF.
A: Ka = c*alpha^2/(1-alpha) gives II. B: [H+] = sqrt(Ka*c) gives IV. C: alpha = sqrt(Ka/c) gives III. D: [OH-] = sqrt(Kb*c) gives I.

A is true: successive Ka values decrease. B is true: Ka1 >> Ka2, so H+ comes mainly from the first step. C is false: a lower pKa means a stronger acid. D is true: pKa + pKb = pKw = 14 at 298 K. E is false: HF is the weakest hydrohalic acid because the H–F bond is strong. Correct set is A, B and D.
[OH-] = 1e-3 M, so pOH = 3 and pH = 14 - 3 = 11.
HCl = 10 mmol and NaOH = 5 mmol, leaving 5 mmol H+ in 100 mL. [H+] = 0.05 M, so pH = 2 - 0.30 = 1.3.
Water's own ionisation must be included. Solve x^2 + 1e-8 x - 1e-14 = 0, giving [H+] ≈ 1.05e-7 M and pH ≈ 6.98.
A is true: Kw rises with temperature, so pH < 7, but [H+] = [OH-] keeps water neutral. R is false: self-ionisation is endothermic, not exothermic.
I is false: pH 2 has 100 times higher [H+] than pH 4. II is false: on dilution the pH only approaches 7 and never exceeds it.
CH3COONa is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base. CH3COO- hydrolyses to give OH-, so the solution is basic. NH4Cl and CuSO4 give acidic solutions; NaCl gives a neutral one.
For a salt of a weak acid and strong base, pH = 7 + 1/2(pKa + log C) = 7 + 1/2(5 - 2) = 8.5.
Kh = Kw/Kb = 1e-14/1e-5 = 1e-9. h = sqrt(Kh/C) = sqrt(1e-9/0.1) = sqrt(1e-8) = 1e-4.
For a weak acid–weak base salt, pH = 7 + 1/2(pKa - pKb). This has no concentration term, so dilution barely changes the pH. A is false and R is true.

Statement I: for CH3COONa, h = sqrt(Kh/C), so dilution increases the degree of hydrolysis; I is incorrect. Statement II: for CH3COONH4, h is independent of concentration, but Kh = Kw/(KaKb) depends on temperature; II is incorrect.
Hg2Cl2 dissolves to Hg2^2+ (s) + 2Cl- (2s), so Ksp = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3.
For MX2, Ksp = 4s^3 = 3.2e-11. Then s^3 = 8e-12, so s = 2.0e-4 M.
Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration to 5e-5 M. Q = (5e-5)^2 = 2.5e-9, which is below Ksp = 5e-9, so no precipitate forms.
AgCl (1:1) gives Ksp = s^2. Ag2CrO4 (2:1) gives 4s^3. Al(OH)3 (1:3) gives 27s^4. A2B3 gives (2s)^2(3s)^3 = 108s^5.

A is true. B is false: Ag2CrO4 has s = 1e-4 M, AgCl has s = 1e-5 M, so Ag2CrO4 is more soluble despite the smaller Ksp. C is true (common ion effect). D is true (acid removes the anion). E is false: the salt with lower Ksp precipitates first. Correct set is A, C, D.
A buffer needs a weak acid plus its conjugate base. CH3COOH with CH3COONa is the only such pair; the others pair a strong acid or strong base with a salt.
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(0.20/0.02) = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74.
HCl converts 0.1 mol NH4OH to NH4Cl, leaving 0.2 mol NH4OH and 0.1 mol NH4Cl in 1 L. pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]) = 4.74 + log(0.1/0.2) = 4.74 − 0.30 = 4.44. pH = 14 − 4.44 = 9.56.
Dilution lowers salt and acid concentrations by the same factor, so their ratio and the pH stay essentially unchanged. A is true. R is false because the ratio does not increase.
Buffer capacity is greatest when [salt] = [acid], i.e. pH = pKa, so I is correct. A ratio of 100 does give pH 6.74, but that lies outside the effective range pKa ± 1, so II is incorrect.
